title: Meditation in the Trees, Metta Practice
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of approaching all beings, including nature, with kindness and compassion, recognizing our interconnectedness and shared humanity. This means cultivating a sense of empathy and understanding that transcends individual boundaries, allowing us to connect with others on a deeper level. By doing so, we can heal the "Wound of the Heart" that often leads to feelings of disconnection and isolation, and instead experience love, compassion, and unity with ourselves and others.

sentences.text: And unsurpassed, penetrating, and perfect dharma is to see and listen to, to remember and accept Tathagata's words.
Good evening.
In the time of the Buddha, a group of his monks who were looking for a comfortable and a safe place for their practice went to meditate in the forest.
We think of the landscape of the Buddha as a forested world, with mountains to the north and plains far off to the south, a land of rich agriculture and not at all a desert.
The Buddha spent his early years of seeking, walking through forests, fields and mountains, and his enlightenment occurred under the protection of a tree.
For a long time after his death, it wasn't appropriate to use the Buddha's actual likeness in the stone-cut art, and instead the image of a tree was often used.
Back then, it was typical practice for the Buddha's disciples to seek out a secluded grove to settle in for practice.
It could be helpful to have a nearby village where they could collect alms.
The villagers would protect the grove from cutting, and thereby also protect the benefaction of the good energy the monks would generate there through their practice.
It was in a reciprocal conception, an ancient form of land protection: if we protect nature, nature will promote enlightenment for us.
But in this case, these monks did not feel any of this sense of reciprocity with the forest they had entered.
It seemed to them instead that the trees were somehow infected by, or perhaps were themselves, malevolent spirits with bad intent towards them.
It seemed they were making painful and horrible sounds, grating, rasping, and scraping noises.
This did not feel like a safe or peaceful place at all.
Instead, the monks felt intensely scared and threatened.
So, in horror, they ran from there quickly, wide-eyed, hair raised, and went straight back to the Buddha for instructions.

The Buddha listened to their story, where they recounted the disturbing noises and how scared they were, and then he gave them his directive: they were to go back to the grove and continue their practice.
"No, we're frightened," begged the monks.
So the Buddha explained to them then that it was actually the trees of the forest who were the frightened ones.
He told the monks that the trees were wounded beings caught in a world of delusion and pain, and were in need of the monks' practice so they might find peace.
The Buddha then instructed the monks on how to act and practice in the presence of such suffering beings.
We're familiar with what he said.
I'll recount a different translation than what we're used to, and in that way we can hear the words a little fresher.
He said, *This is what should be done by those who are skilled in goodness and who know the path of peace.

Let them be able and upright, straightforward and gentle in speech, humble and not conceited, contented and easily satisfied, unburdened with duties and frugal in their ways, peaceful and calm and wise and skillful, not proud and demanding in nature.
Let them do nothing, not the slightest thing that the wise would later reprove.

Wishing in their minds, in gladness and in safety, may all beings be at ease, whatever living beings there may be, whether they are weak or strong, omitting none, the great or the mighty, medium, short or small, the seen and the unseen.
Those living near and far away, those born and to be born, may all beings be at ease.
Let none deceive another or despise any being in any state.
Let none through anger or ill will wish harm upon another.

Even as a mother protects with her life, her child, her only child, so with a boundless heart should one cherish all living beings, radiating kindness over the entire world, spreading upward to the skies and downward to the depths, outward and unbounded, free from hatred and ill will.
Whether standing or walking, seated or lying down, free from drowsiness, one should sustain this recollection.
This is said to be the sublime abiding.*
By not holding to fixed views, the pure-hearted one, having clarity of vision, being freed from all sense desires, is not born again into this world.
We, of course, came from the forest, monkey beings, swinging with our tails from the tree limbs, using our good focal depth binocular vision to judge the distance for the next leap.
Trees are our friends, and the forest is our home.
In many ways, we can see ourselves in trees, in their individuality, and we can see our society in their forest community.
I've been rereading at Scott's suggestion Peter Wolbin's great book, *The Hidden Life of Trees*.
I brought a little stack of books; this is just my thing, a book stack person.
In it, Wolbin talks about becoming aware, after many years as a forest manager in Germany, that there was much more to the forest he was managing than he had first assumed.
As he began to allow his imagination to shift, he realized that for a long time, he'd been viewing the forest through a set of assumptions that simply were not fitting his observations.
Forest, meaning the trees, really, in particular, are not just passive groupings.

More properly seen, they are actively cooperative, extended families, and neighborhoods of mixed relations, intimately woven together through many dimensions of mutual communication and sharing of resources.
Wolbin discovered that a forest, although made up of individuals, is wired together at all levels, especially in the soil.
Roots intertwine and nutrients are shared from the strong to the weak, so the whole forest can thrive together and maintain the collective humidity and wind protection that protects them all.
Neural networks are mimicked through vast mass of fungal filaments, mycelia that hardwire the communication pathways between the roots.
Pheromones drift downwind from trees, undergoing insect pressure so as to warn their neighbors so that they may produce toxic exodus, which can ward off the invaders.
So once Wolbin began seeing the forest this way, he also noticed something which really caused him to wonder about the kind of affinity that trees may have towards each other.
The first insight was that trees live with their family members for their whole lives.
It seems obvious when we think about it.
But when he found that some small objects on the ground he had long assumed were stones, were actually remnant bits of a huge ancient stump ring, he made a startling discovery.
The wood of the old stump, nearly buried in the ground from a tree felled perhaps 500 years before, was still alive.
It was being fed from below ground by interconnected roots from the old trees children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren.
That the younger trees would expend energy to keep tiny remnants of an elder alive did not make conventional ecological sense in terms of energy flow.
The only reason he could imagine was that the continued connection was one of affinity.
The big takeaway from reading *The Hidden Life of Trees* is that this entire world of separate and distinct individuals is connected into one community.
In the forest, obviously, but if there, then just as likely everywhere, and certainly by means we can barely figure out.
But of all the means, the most essential is undeniably not a physical connection, but rather the fundamental principles of affection and affinity, cooperation, and compassion themselves.
Beyond communication pathways of sound, taste, and sight, smell, and touch, there is simple affinity that is connecting it all together.
We love the mountain's form, and so we look up.
We hear the raven calling out to the whole world, telling everyone the news.
So not unlike trees, even our very existence proceeds directly out of the existence of another.
And so also those that come after us come also from us.
In space and through time, we are truly not alone, and we never can be.
But in living out our individual separate lives and caught within our individual separate pains and dramas, we seem to believe just the opposite.

It seems that in our guts, before anything we may think, we believe our existential outlook is that we are fundamentally unknown, disconnected, and all alone in getting through this life without any help.
Although keen observation of nature tells us the opposite, we find ourselves unable to shake off the fear of isolation and the idea that this world will not support us.
We are like the monks when they first enter the forest.
We see this world in a reflection, of course, as a projection of the fears about ourselves that we hold inside.

Thinking about how we tend to do this, and why, and wondering, I found myself thumbing through another book on my shelf, *Perfect Love, Imperfect Relationships*, by the psychotherapist John Wellwood, *Healing the Wound of the Heart*.
It's funny, I've had that book for years, and a couple times I've looked at it and not connected with it, and this time it suddenly all made sense.
It's a good reason to keep around a book if you think it's got something you don't understand.
He has this term called the Wound of the Heart, and he describes it as universal.
We all have this.
His thinking goes like this: we can all well imagine how abusive, negligent, or absent parenting would lead us to having some real problems with intimacy and relationships later in life, right?
But even with seemingly near-perfect parenting, we're guaranteed to have many moments in our upbringing when love wasn't given in some important way and we felt we really needed it.
And we may often, in certain situations, get praise or appreciation, but despite this, we still hardly ever feel we are seen for who we believe we really are, even by those closest to us.
So a tricky little thing happens within us, because feeling this disconnection from being loved the way we really need to be is painful.
We do what just seems natural: we turn away from that, we shut that down, cover it over, explain it away, or try to stop feeling that.
Like the monks, we run out of the forest.
But in this case, the forest is our whole life, so there's really nowhere to run to.
So instead, we just imagine to ourselves that all that pain doesn't actually exist.
The psychological term Wellwood uses is dissociation, which leads to what he calls this wound of the heart.
He describes it as not knowing we're loved as we are, then numbing our heart to ward off this pain, thereby shutting down the pathways through which love can flow into and through us.
He makes it sound like tree roots.
So the Buddha apparently totally understood this.
He understood that the world is full of suffering beings, all inextricably connected and codependent, but all deluded in a dream of isolation and unlove.

And he understood that the way to deal with this can only begin with our individual selves undoing the way we habitually turn away from our pain of unlove, finding a way through our own fears and senses of inadequacy, by reminding ourselves of our own goodness, steadfastness, and peace, and then, by natural extension, following the roots of our connections, extending our practice outward to hold forth the same wish towards others, to uncover and realize their inherent safety, happiness, and goodness.
So this is the exact instruction he gave the monks: first, understand that this is what should be accomplished.
We have this work to do, and it is a task which must be done.

Then we're instructed to first remember our innate wisdom, our sense of goodness, our own lifelong effort toward more peacefulness, our sense of integrity, our ability to be gentle, humble, satisfied, and basically free from obligations and expectation and any other judgmental ideas we may hold about who we imagine we should be rather than who we know we are.
With nothing to prove to anyone, we can live without pride, easily contented in joyous feeling.
Feeling the security, the safety of love, we then can extend a wish outward to this world of suffering beings: be happy, live in safety, be trusting, feel kindness.

We can do this for all beings in all places at all times, beginning with what is very near to us, the people you hold close, to the people you don't know, from the people you love to the people you can barely stand to think of, from the friend right here in front of you to the farthest mote of matter in the completely gone beyond universe at space.
So this is called metapractice, and the talk the Buddha gave to the monks is known, of course, as the Metta Sutta.

It's a practice centered within the treasure of sangha, the natural support of interconnection and affinity that exists between all things in this existence because the practice literally involves weaving together and healing all the relationships we have with others but also within ourselves through affinity and affection.
And the Buddha claimed that this was a complete practice, immeasurable in its benefits and expansion.
You can do this as a seated meditation practice where you quietly recount these phrases of encouragement to yourself in visualization.
And there are many sources that lay out specific phrases and techniques.
I've just sort of given an outline here.
But I've got another book that is one of the best books on this subject that I know, *Loving Kindness* by Sharon Salzberg.
So I really recommend this book if you're interested in this idea.

But it begins with and probably always goes back to the part that is certainly hardest for all of us, and that is the part of accepting, feeling kindness for, expressing safety for, and loving ourselves.

That part of the practice will certainly evoke resistances like unpleasant noises, ideas about our worthiness or our goodness that cause us to want to run away and reconfirm our protections and avoidances.
It may appear from the natural habit we have of turning away from unloved that we are alone and not worthy of self-love or perhaps even of love coming to us from without.
But this world accepts us and supports us.
We live in the forest of this world.
And when seen with fearlessness and wisdom, it is clear that this world reflects back to us how lovely we are.

Because the world is completely full, without exception, of suffering beings just like ourselves, we are all equally connected in an inseparable sangha and all trying to find peace through a rooted connection of love.
We are not alone.
Some years ago I helped lead some folks on a pilgrimage journey.
We spent two weeks hiking seventy-five miles around the Three Sisters in Oregon.
Three mountains, each the height of Mount Baker, but so close together that you can walk around the mall.
And my old hiking buddy, Rick, retired recently and he founded a new literary journal.
He put out the first edition of that just a couple months ago.
And I was lucky enough to place an essay in here about that trip.
And I realized there were a couple things that I said in here that relate.
And I'm going to donate this book to the library.
In the almost black twilight of early morning I am walking through a dark forest, rhythmically ringing a small bell.
I'm searching for a tent but I don't know where it is.
Below me mist floats suspended in the pre-dawn gray over Damaris Lake.
As I step over yet another crumbled log, the barren, littered understory of the forest feels trackless and dreamlike.
An image comes to me of lazily swimming in a subalpine lake in the sun nearly two weeks ago and on the other side of the ten-thousand foot mountain above our camp.
But it feels like a memory from some other year.
How many days have I been walking?
How many mornings now has all this wildness held its settled composure, silently mirroring each trembling flicker of my mind?
As I walk forward, each sounding of the bell dies in the darkness, barely penetrating the fog.
I still don't know where the tent is.
So it seems there's nothing to do but just keep walking, gently waking up people, waking up the whole world.
Later that morning we're packed for the trail, but before leaving we have a final task.
It's our Sangha day.
And so we head out to a nearby escarpment overlooking the far-off horizons of eastern Oregon, where sunlight spreads across wide golden lands beyond seeing.
The drifting light and shadow below beckons to us up in our high, cold forest.

Lighting a candle and incense and ringing the bell, we perform prostrations to the immensity of it all and enchant a series of sacred texts, well-wishes and prayers for the betterment of all beings as we chant in the Metta Sutta, suffusing love over the entire world, above, below, and all around without limit.
May our intentions equally extend to every being.
